questions.q: What are the five principles of Panchsheel, and in which year was the agreement signed between India and China?
questions.a: The five principles are: (1) Mutual respect for each other’s territorial integrity and sovereignty, (2) Mutual non-aggression, (3) Mutual non-interference in internal affairs, (4) Equality and mutual benefit, (5) Peaceful coexistence. Signed on 29 April 1954. A wrong answer (e.g., listing "non-alignment" as a principle or citing 1950) reveals confusion between Panchsheel and the broader Non-Aligned Movement, or ignorance of the exact diplomatic milestone.

questions.q: Why did India concede China’s claim over Tibet in the 1954 Panchsheel Agreement, and how did this concession later become a source of tension?
questions.a: India conceded Tibet to secure Chinese goodwill and operationalise Panchsheel, believing Tibet’s autonomy would be preserved. The concession became a flashpoint when China suppressed the 1958 Tibetan uprising and the Dalai Lama fled to India in 1959 — Beijing then accused India of harbouring "anti-China activities," turning a diplomatic gesture into a sovereignty dispute. A student who says "India always supported Tibetan independence" misunderstands the 1954 concession; one who says "Tibet was never an issue" ignores the 1959 asylum as a direct war catalyst.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "security dilemma" to explain why China built a strategic road through Aksai Chin (1957–59) and how India’s discovery of it escalated the border dispute.
questions.a: China built the Xinjiang-Tibet highway through Aksai Chin to consolidate control over Tibet — a legitimate security need from Beijing’s perspective. India, however, viewed Aksai Chin as part of Ladakh (Johnson Line) and saw the road as a military threat to its northern frontier. Neither side accepted the other’s cartographic claim (India: Johnson/Ardagh lines; China: "traditional customary line"), creating a classic security dilemma: defensive infrastructure by one side perceived as offensive by the other. A wrong answer that blames only one side ("China was expansionist" or "India provoked") fails to grasp the structural misperception central to IR analysis.

questions.q: Analyse how the 1962 war transformed India’s domestic politics in three specific ways: (a) executive accountability, (b) party system, (c) federal restructuring.
questions.a: (a) Executive accountability: First no-confidence motion against Nehru (August 1963), Defence Minister V.K. Krishna Menon forced to resign — rare instance of parliamentary scrutiny of foreign policy failure. (b) Party system: CPI split in 1964 into CPI (pro-USSR) and CPI(M) (pro-China), reshaping the Left’s electoral trajectory. (c) Federal restructuring: Nagaland granted statehood (1963); Manipur and Tripura given legislative assemblies — direct response to Northeast’s vulnerability exposed by the war. A student listing only "Nehru lost popularity" misses the institutional and structural consequences.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The 1962 war was a failure of Nehru’s foreign policy, not a failure of non-alignment." Support your judgment with two arguments for and two against.
questions.a: For: (1) Nehru’s personal assurance that China would not attack ("exceedingly unlikely") reflected naive threat assessment, not non-alignment’s fault. (2) Military neglect (paramilitary guarding border, no modern arms) was a domestic policy choice. Against: (1) Non-alignment limited India’s access to Western military hardware until the war forced US/UK aid — strategic autonomy had a cost. (2) The Bandung/NAM focus on Afro-Asian solidarity blinded India to China’s realist nationalism. A balanced evaluation recognises that non-alignment provided diplomatic space but could not substitute for deterrence. A one-sided answer ("Nehru failed" or "non-alignment failed") shows inability to weigh structural vs. agency factors.

questions.q: Create a diplomatic note (150 words) that Prime Minister Nehru might have written to Zhou Enlai in January 1963, after the ceasefire, proposing a mechanism to prevent future border clashes — incorporating lessons from the war.
questions.a: A strong note would: (1) Acknowledge the ceasefire as a basis for dialogue, (2) Propose a Joint Boundary Commission with access to historical maps (Johnson, McMahon, Chinese "traditional" lines), (3) Suggest a demilitarised zone (DMZ) in disputed sectors pending settlement, (4) Link border peace to broader Panchsheel revival, (5) Offer reciprocal troop withdrawals verified by neutral observers. A weak answer repeats "peaceful coexistence" slogans without concrete mechanisms (DMZ, commission, verification), showing inability to translate principles into operational diplomacy.
